newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: John Fairfax year net seen down 11 pct.
newsitem.headline: John Fairfax year net seen down 11 pct.

text.p: Newspaper publisher John Fairfax Holdings Ltd is expected to report on Tuesday that slow economic growth and advertising volumes through late 1996 pushed net profit down about about 11 percent in the 1996/97 year.
Analysts said however that the market focus would be on how much advertising had recovered a trough seen in the third quarter of the year to June 30.
"Advertising volumes appeared to have bottomed in the third quarter, but we'll be interested to know how things have picked up and what the outlook is like," a Melbourne analyst said.
Analysts' forecasts for Fairfax's net profit before abnormals range from A$75.1 million to A$99.4 million, with a median forecast of A$90.3 million, according to BZW's Barceps survey.
Fairfax reported a A$102 million net profit before abnormals in the 1995/96 year, down from A$145 million in 1994/95 because of higher paper costs.
Net profits after abnormals in 1995/96 fell 40.6 percent to A$87.43 million.
Profits remained weak in the first half of the just-completed year, with net profit before abnormals falling 24.7 percent to A$46.95 million on a slight sales fall.
Analysts said the growth-sensitive advertising market had remained relatively moribund in the second half as the economy failed to respond to interest rate cuts in late 1995.

"The issue is that business conditions have been fairly poor for them and we're starting to see some recovery in their volumes now, but probably at levels not quite as healthy as one would wish," said one Sydney media analyst.
"I don't think they're showing any robust growth," he said, adding he was forecasting a pre-abnormal net of A$87.5 million.
Analysts also said they would examine the likely profit effects of Fairfax's current expansion plans.

These include the Saturday edition of The Australian Financial Review due to start on September 6 and the Good Weekend magazine issued with the Saturday Sydney Morning Herald which was revamped last weekend.
Fairfax's largest shareholder is Brierley Investments Ltd, which said in mid June it had increased its stake to 22.09 percent from 19.98 percent.
It did so under the "creep" provisions that allow a company to increase its stake three percent every six months without having to launch a full takeover bid.
Without this provision, a company would have to launch a full takeover bid once over 20 percent.
The Australian Securities Commission said however on Friday it was investigating swap arrangements undertaken in March by Brierley Investments and Merrill Lynch over a 4.9 percent stake in Fairfax.
